messages.subject: (from stan-users): inferring array length
parts:
There was a discussion on stan-users about inferring
array lengths. Andrew had wanted something like this, too.

I argued that I rather like the declarations and Ben
provided an example. The rest's inline.

On 10/10/12 1:22 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, October 10, 2012 12:48:44 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > It sounds like a reasonable request, but I'm not immediately seeing how to make it work on the C++ side.
> Maybe the
> > C++ file stan() generates could #define NROW__ and let this .stan syntax
> >
> > |
> > data {
> > real<lower=0> rate[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
> > real<lower=0> conc[]; // implicitly using NROW__ as the length
> > }
> > |
> >
> > be valid. Andrew would probably like it and Bob would probably hate it. We'll see.
>
> I'll reserve judgment until I can figure out how
> something like this could be made to work!
>
>
> I was imagining that the above would parse as
>
> |
> rate = std::vector<double>(NROW__,double(0));
> if (!context__.contains_r("rate"))
> throw std::runtime_error("variable rate not found.");
> vals_r__ = context__.vals_r("rate");
> pos__ = 0;
> size_t rate_limit_0__ = NROW__;
> for (size_t i_0__ = 0; i_0__ < rate_limit_0__; ++i_0__) {
> rate[i_0__] = vals_r__[pos__++];
> }

> Basically, my imagined rule would be "if the length is unspecified in the .stan file, assume it is NROW__ in the .cpp
> file". But the logic probably would need to be fleshed out more to deal with corner cases, and even then, I am assuming
> you and Andrew would disagree.

How would NROW__ be set? That's the part I couldn't see.

> For a variety of reasons, it might be good to have a block in the .stan file that was pasted literally into the .cpp
> file after the #includes but before anything else.

I was thinking that would also be useful for includes.
I still haven't finalized the design for that and am
going to run some options by the list soon.

Something like
>
> |
> literal code {
> #define N 1000
> }
> data {
> real<lower=0> rate[N];
> real<lower=0> conc[N];
> }
> |
>
> could compile faster than the usual
>
> |
> data {
> int<lower=1> N;
> real<lower=0> rate[N];
> real<lower=0> conc[N];
> }
> |
>
> because the compiler could allocate a bunch of stuff at compile time instead of runtime. Although that would mean the
> binary wouldn't work if you wanted to pass different samples to it, and there would be no bounds on N to check.

I'm afraid the [N] get compiled to std::vector,
which can't allocate statically.

It would be a bad idea to put this kind of thing
on the stack (which is where static allocs go) because
the stack is limited in size.

I now realize I don't where variables declared
at global scope get allocated. If that's a separate
non-stack space, that could work.

> The literal code block could also be used to define implicit functions if we supported that some day.

I still need to understand how that works. I worked
through some examples of implicit integrators for
Hamiltonian simulation.

- Bob

How would NROW__ be set?  That's the part I couldn't see.

I was imagining that stan() would always insert

#define NROW__

into the .cpp file, whether it were used or not, based on the length of the largest thing that was passed to it in data. I'm not seeing how it would work for command-line stan unless there were a literal block, and even then, it has issues like you mentioned.

> The literal code block could also be used to define implicit functions if we supported that some day.

I still need to understand how that works.  I worked
through some examples of implicit integrators for
Hamiltonian simulation.

I don't know what exactly the stochastic differential equation guy had in mind, but here is a simple but unlikely example. Suppose you have a parameter alpha, and you need a transformed parameter beta that goes into the likelihood. And you know that

beta^5 - beta = alpha

Given alpha, it may be possible to numerically find one value of beta on an interval that satisfies this equation. There might be problems if there are multiple solutions, but sometimes there is only one solution. In any event, it is impossible to write beta as an explicit function of alpha in the transformed parameters {} block. It may be possible to do something like

literal code {
  template<typename T>
  const T find_beta(const T alpha, const double lower, const double upper) {
    double alpha_double = alpha;
    // find the value of beta that is a root of an implicit function
    const T beta = whatever;
    return beta;
  }
}
data {
  // something
}
parameters {
  real alpha;
}
implicit transformations {
  real<lower,upper> beta;
  beta <- find_beta(alpha, lower, upper);
}

In HMC you ultimately need the derivative of the log-posterior with respect to alpha. That is knowable from the derivative of the log-posterior with respect to beta and the derivative of beta with respect to alpha, but those rules would need to be programmed into Stan somehow.

Maybe more relevant, eigenvalues can be seen as the roots of det(Sigma - lambda * I) = 0, and so you can use the gradient of lambda with respect to the parameters that generated Sigma to circumvent a ton of auto-diff.

Ben

parts:
On Wednesday, October 10, 2012 4:49:14 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I was imagining that stan() would always insert
>
> #define NROW__

Yes, but how does the value get assigned?
Inside R, we know the (maximum) length of the stuff being passed in the data list. So, stan() could just glue a #define on top of the .cpp file after stanc makes it but before it is compiled.

> I don't know what exactly the stochastic differential equation guy had in mind, but here is a simple but unlikely
> example. Suppose you have a parameter alpha, and you need a transformed parameter beta that goes into the likelihood.
> And you know that
>
> beta^5 - beta = alpha

I see.  This is very general.  I thought there'd
be some probability distribution or something that
would need this.  Is there a simple applied example
within my grasp?

Actually, there are probability distributions that need implicit differentiation but that would usually entail us writing C++ rather than getting it from the user. There are many distributions where the quantile function (inverse of CDF) is known in closed form, but the PDF (and CDF) are not known in closed form. For example,

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tukey_lambda_distribution

The deal with these things is that you can explicitly write the density in terms of the quantile (the proportion of the mass to the left of x) but not in terms of x. So, given x, you have to numerically solve for the corresponding quantile and then evaluate the density. And then, in the HMC context, get the right gradient because the quantile that is a root of the implicit function is in turn a function of the unknown parameters.

This is actually an area where Stan could make a big contribution. These distributions that are defined by quantile functions are very flexible, but they don't get used much in the literature because the density is not available in the closed form. So, calculating the MLEs is hard, and doing Gibbs sampling is impossible.

> Maybe more relevant, eigenvalues can be seen as the roots of det(Sigma - lambda * I) = 0, and so you can use the
> gradient of lambda with respect to the parameters that generated Sigma to circumvent a ton of auto-diff.

I'll have to think about that one.  I didn't see anythning
to do with eigenvalues analytically in the Matrix Cookbook,
but I should look at Magnus and Neudecker, too.

The eigenvalues are not known analytically; the derivatives of the eigenvalues with respect to the parameters are known analytically (but are a function of the eigenvectors). Here is a reference

http://gifi.stat.ucla.edu/janspubs/2007/reports/deleeuw_R_07c.pdf

Ben

In Doug's example, I don't think he was considering using a multidimensional array. But I don't think it is worth changing the language that much. If the user forgets to pass N or K or something, the error message is unambiguous and as of 1.0.3 stan() will return a stanfit object with no results but a valid binary. So, the user can quickly fix the data list.

Ben
